Before parting with the Marquis of SALIS.

which it would be amiss not to point out. "It
was," he said,
," becoming every year less and
less important who held the seals of power;
but day by day it was becoming more and
more important who occupied the House of
Commons. What the House of Commons was,
so would the Ministry be." This is not only
true, but it is a truth worth remembering and
acting on. It plainly indicates how the
policies of administrations are influenced, and
how the law under which we live is shaped.
The opinions, the prejudices, or even the power
of the Heim of Lords are 'disregarded by 'the
MLietarea of the Cnower when any really im
portant Measure for the country has to be,
passed. The majority of the House of Com-
mons, backed by the people who sent them,
direct the policy of the Government; and on
this hint the, Liberal electors of England must
act, when the fitting opportunity arises., Lord
SALISBURY knows that he and his party are
engaged in a losing game, so long as they
simply try to play off the privileged classes

policy try to make the people minister to their
own defeat, by following blindfold the banners
of their party as " operative Conservatives."

stupid parliamentary dummies who call them-
selves Liberals, under fear of " splitting the

Mu Marquis of SALISBURY is, beyond
doubt, one of the ablest and, it may be added,
one of the most honest men belonging to the
Conservative 'party. He has a very high
opinion of himself and his position, as well
as lofty notions as to the rights and privileges
of those extremely lucky creatures called
British Peers. It would be of no use to
object to this. The public generally care very
little as to what he may think of himself or
his order. Considering, however, that he is a
man looked up to by his party, that he can
utter in the clearest way the settled and
definite policy of that party, so far as it is
within the power of human comprehension,
people peruse with interest whatever he has to
say, and search in it for events to come—in
connection with the political life of the
country—as the augurs of old sought to fore..
east the future by carefully examining the
entrails of holy chickens.
The speech of the noble MARQUIS at the
dinner of the Dorsetshire Conservative Asso-
ciation the other day was a good, specimen of
words without definite meaning; hints that
pointed nowhere or everywhere; explanations
in themselves inexplicable; hopes for his
party, or for his country, only through his
party; praises and censures full of admira-
tion and anger, but withuut the recommenda-
tion of common sense or common fairness. He
assured his hearers that the' Whigs were
willing to tolerate the House of Lords if it
did not interfere with the House of Commons.
In admitting this he paid the Whigs too high
a compliment. The Whigs are as anxious
to preserve the House of Lords as are the
Tories; but they have sense enough to see
that it cannot be preserved if it doggedly
antagonises the will of the nation. The
question, in truth, is not a Whig and Tory
question. It is a question between the nation
and a privileged class; and if the nation and
this class cannot act together without coming
into collision as opposing forces, there ought
not to be two opinions as to the way in which
the contest will end. The general body of
the public, we think, have no fear on this
head; and the less said about the matter by
the Marquis of SALISBURY and others like
him, the better it will be for the institution he
is so anxious to preserve, but over the term of
whose existence he has no more power than
the summer fly has over the progress of the
Bun.

servative policy, or rather his policy; but

tinct, so meaningless, that the matter may
be said to rest precisely where it was
before he touched it. The most important

articles.title: DORSET LABOURERS.
articles.text:
THE DORSET LABOURERS.

An enthusiastic meeting of the agricultural
labourers of Dorset was held at the Corn Exchange,
Dorchester, on Tuesday evening. Nearly 1,000
persons were present, the chair being occupied by
Mr. Snook, of Whitechurch. The following reso-
lution was passed
That this meeting, while it in no way wishes to
create feelings of hostility between employers and
employed, is of opinion that the National Agri-
cultural Labourers' Union deserves the confidence
and support of the agricultural labourers of this
county, and especially pledges itself to exertits best
efforts on its behalf.

The Hon. Auberon Herbert, M.P., then spoke
on the benefits of unionism, urging that it was a
privilege to unite together and protect themselves.
These unions, he said, had spent thousands of
pounds in mitigating the hardships and accidents
of life, and thus promoted a spirit of self-reliance
and independence; they were governed in an order-
ly, wise, and prudent manner, and were therefore
deserving of every confidence and support. Ho
recommended migration, urging that the labourers
should never cease their agitation until they were
on equal ground with the farmers. They must be
perfectly free men. Speeches wore then delivered
by Mr. Alliugton and Mr. Alsop, of Warwick, and
others, during which it was contended that the
bard hoartedness of Dorset employers was not to
be equalled in England. Emigration to Brazil was
recommended, it being stated that the Government
of that country was prepared to assist .500,000 men
in going there from England. The meeting adopt-
ed a petition to Parliament praying for the as-
similation of the county to the borough franchise,
a thorough redistribution of seats, and a fairer
representation of the penile. The proceedings
were of an enthusiastic character. On Wednesday
the Hon. Auboron Herbert addressed a similar
meeting at Wimborne Minster, in the same county.

THE SOUTH WALES COLLIERS.

A delegate meeting representing the colliers and
ironstone ruiners of South Wales and Monmouth-
shire, was held at Merthyr Tydfil on Wednesday,
to consider what steps should be taken in view of
the notices which were given by the ironmasters
and coalowners on Saturday last for a reduction of
10 per cont. It was resolved to resist the pro-

claim 010 per cent. The men contend that the
present market quotations do not justify any re-
duction in, the standard of wages. It was also
agreed that a deputation should wait upon the
masters, requesting that the dispute should be re-
ferred to arbitration. A strike on the Ist of January
next is considered inevitable.

articles.title: LONDON TRADES COUNCIL.
articles.text:
THE LONDON TRADES COUNCIL.

A special meeting of the London Trades Council
was held on Tuesday night at the Bell Inn, Old
Bailey, Mr. Warren in the chair.
Mr. Shipton, the secretary, read the letter which
he had received from Mr. Cardwell in reference
to the employment of soldiers in the harvest fields
in the place of Union labourers locked out, and
which has already been published.
Mr. Odger considered the letter and the pledge
of Mr. Cardwell contained therein—that in future
soldiers should not be employed so as to interfere
with any existing dispute between the labourers
and their employers —as satisfactory. He
moved—

That the letter of Mr. Cardwell be accepted by
the Council as perfectly satisfactory, and that the
secretary write to Mr. Cardwell to that effect.

Mr. Proggatt seconded the resolution, which
after some discussion, was adopted.
The secretary road a letter from the Council of
the Labourers' Union at Leamington, acknowledg-
ing the receipt of £5O, from the Trades Council,
and stating that they had forwarded that amount
to the labourers in Dorset, where 300 were out of
employment. Several other li.tters were read
stating that there was a weekly emigration of
labourers on a large scale, and that by nest spring

their ranks would be so reduced as to insure to
those remaining the concession of their claims.
A resolution was then adopted, that the Council
should attend the meeting announced for next
week at Exeter-hall on behalf of the agricultural
labourers.

The question of appointing delegates to represent
the Council at the forthcoming Trades Congress
at Leeds was then considered, and it was resolved
that a special delegate meeting of all the trades
connected with the Council should be held on
Tuesday, the 17th inst., for the purpose of appoint-
ing the delegates. The question of sending
another sum of money to the Leamington Council
of the Labourers' Union was also deferred to the
above meeting.

articles.title: WASTE AND WASTED LANDS.
articles.text:
WASTE AND WASTED LANDS.

Having recently visited the north of Scot-
land (says a correspondent of the Manchester
Examiner and Times) I have been appalled at
seeing the vast extent of land appropriated to
deer and grouse. Here are thousands of acres ,
of land comparatively useless, yet capable of
cultivation, and of supplying the wants of oar
people. I passed the remains of old homesteads
and cottages in ruins. What is the remedy for
this state of things? What are the limitations
to a man doing as he likes with his land?
What laws are there which prevent great
estates from being broken up and sold in lots?
Is it not the duty of Government to try and
increase the products of the soil, and see that
uncultivated lands, which can be cultivated,
should be so employed? Would it not be right
for Government to say to landed proprietors,
"You have so many thousands of acres capable
of supplying food, which are now next to
useless; you must either cultivate them your
self or we will buy them from you at a fair
price, and sell them to those who will cultivate
them ?" Taking for granted that Great Britain
is the richest country in the world, and that
there is also more abject poverty in it than
any other country, I further ask, " What effect
has the curtailment of the area of cultivation
(for the mere protection of game) on the wealth
and happiness of the community at large P
Have the people no rights in respect to uncul-
tivated land, which override mere proprietorial
rights ?"

articles.title: PIECEWORK IN AGRICULTURE.

PIECEWORK IN AGRICULTURE.

Lord Nelson, in an address which his lord-
ship has recently circulated among his tenantry
of Whiteparisb, in Wilts, says:—" I press
you to give piecework ,for everything, winter
and summer. Turning, spreading, and cast-
ing dung will all come into piecework. You
will not pay a farthing more for the quality of
the work done. You will be enabling the best
men to earn what they are really worth, and
you will be educating and bringing up e
better style of labour. What can be worse
policy than to keep an active young man,
under twenty, at a lower wage then his elder,
simply because they are older or may be
married men ? Piecework at once cures thr
evil, and enables the young man to hold his
own when he has the ability and desire to lay
by. I know it can be done so as to raise the
wages to a clear 14s. throughout the year,
without counting the wife's or children's earn-
ings, and if it can he made to pay in one case
why can't it in all? But if piecework is to
educate the labourer he must be kept con-
tinuously on one farm, and I must plead for
the same hands being kept on, both winter and
summer, if you would really wish to improve
the character and value of the labour of your
district." Piecework has also been strongly re-
commended in similar terms to the farmers of
Dorset.

articles.title: CAPE COLONY. To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.
articles.text:
CAPE COLONY.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

Sfit,—Being one of the many readers of
your mteresting paper I find questions asked
respecting the Cape Colony. Perhaps a few
remarks from one who has been in Cape Town
and its vicinity for several years will be of a
little service to their inquiries.
Ist. The climate in general is spoken of as
being very healthy ; the seasons are the
reverse to ours, and at times during the
summer months the heat is intense, not a
cloud in the horizon or a breeze in the bay,
the water itself looking like quicksilver; then
suddenly you will perceive a white cloud
creeping over Table Mountain—at the too tof
which Cape Town is situated. This cloud is
termed the table-cloth, from its white appear-
ance, and in a few minutes the wind rises and
blows with such fury clouds of sand and dust
that out-door business is almost suspended.
These winds continue sometimes for a week
together, and are termed " sou'-easters," or as
the natives say, the Cape Doctor, because they
blow and clear the town of the offensive
smells, as the drainage is not to perfection.
The winter months are passed with very
heavy rains and "nor'-west " gales, though
there are some very fino days during the
season, and very pleasant for out-door
exercise.
2nd. The passage-money, per steamer, £3O
and upwards; sailing ships, £lB to 1:25. The
voyage, one month for steamers, two months
or more for sailing vessels.
3rd. Boarding can be obtained in private
families for £1 is. per week; washing extra.
A person may choose his nation, as there are
all sorts, such as Italians, Germans, Dutch,
Americans, and English. The curry powder
is very much used; in fact, almost every
dish is served up with this native relish. Fish
is also very abundant, the tomato sauce
being another of their favourite dishes. Beef
and mutton is inferior to ours at home; in
fact, I found the food not as substantial as
ours in old England.—l remain, Sir, yours
respectfully,

WALTER COOPER, Mason.
16, West-street, Pimlico, S. \Y.

UNITED KINGDOM SOCIETY OF
COACIIMAKERS.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

Stit,—l see in your paper a letter signed L.
Smith, who I am glad to see has taken up the
cause of the society. But why use personalities?
he must know, if he is an intelligent man,
that when a man takes up a case of this
description, and has reoeurse to personal abuse,
the cause that he advocates must rest on a
very rotten foundation; and if the present
executive committee consist of men of this
stamp, I have not the slighest doubt but that
We should be treated to the following un-
bounded eloquence in our next report:—" We
have now to expose a member who has taken
advantage of the press to expose our rules and
benefits, with a view to give great scandal
and dissatisfaction to our members. It is
with sorrow that we do this thing, but if in-
dividual members cannot place confidence in
119 as the executive committee, we have no
other resource. Finishing with a phrase well
known amongst coachmakers. We hope this
will teach him a lesson he will not forget, and
that he will profit thereby." In my opinion fit
language for a company of imbeciles. How-
ever, we will pass on to the executive, not
placing obstacles in our way. Twelve months
ago, at the request of a number of our mem-
bers, I drew up the following rule :—That any
man having piece-work do show his price
book at least once a week to the shop secretary;
and should he employ one or more men, the
balance over and above the weekly wages be
divided, thus, 10 per cent. to be taken off the
balance for the man who has charge, and the
remainder to be divided according to the
!mount of money each man has drawn on the
job. Any member not obeying this rule be
summoned before the town committee and be
fined for first offence 10s. ; second offence to
be excluded. This was carried by upwards
of 300 members, and was sent down to Liver-
pool for thorn to place before the country,
:ovhen they in reply stated that they did not
intend to allow any alterations until next
November, as that was the proper time. Two
delegates waited on the Manchester committee,
who again sent it down; still the same
answer; when in the next, or next but one
report, they advised an alteration which was
nothing but to benefit private men. So much
for the executive not plating obstacles in the
way. Mr. Smith makes mention of a rule
which states that this society discourages
piece-work, and calls on its members to
abolish it wh-ro practicable. In my opinion
mere waste paper, as it can be used as a cloak
to keep men in ignorance and oppression. As
regards L. Smith's personal abuse of mo,

treat it with silent contempt, and put it down
to the effects of an excited brain; and, as to-
gals the men of Miles Platting, there are few
who are working under the iron heel of a
piece-master, and it is their wish to sweep
the piece-master's system completely away,
both out of the railway and private shops, so
that every member can receive the full benefit
of his labour. Taking his letter on the whole,
he has almost corroborated my statements;
and I may state that it is not my object to
injure the -United Kingdom Society of Coach-
makers, but to get them to alter these rules so
that instead of being at the bottom of the
ladder they way be at the top, and then co-
operate with the railway society.—Yours, &0.,
GEORGE TOOGOOD.

LONDON SCHOOL BOARD.

Several interesting topics occupied the Lon-
don School Board on Wednesday. A proposal
to grant the use of schools for adult evening
classes was made by Mr. Lucraft and agreed
to on condition that no expense should be
thereby entailed on the Board. Motions of
Mr. Macgregor, for the prior accommodation
of neglected children in the schools, and for
compulsory attendance of children until suffi-
cient reason had been shown for the parents'
choice of some other school, were rejected by
large majorities.
Mr. Lafono called attention to the number
of children who were being employed in con-
nection with the Christmas pantomime. He
said that between 800 and .1,000 children
were the other morning surrounding a theatre
on the Surrey side of the water waiting to be
selected. The same kind of thing was going
on in every district of London. A letter was
sent to the Home Seoretary inquiring whether
the children might not be brought under the
operation of the Factory and Workshops Act.
The reply said—" I beg to inform you that in
rehearstug for a performance and performing
at a theatre, children are not exercising any
manual labour by way of trade, and, therefore,
no action can be taken under the Factory Act."
It was agreed that, although the Board could
not move in the matter, some steps ought to
be taken, perhaps by the Education Depart-
ment. .

The Rev. Canon Barry gave the following
notice of motion:—" That, whereas the Board
has directed that, as a general rule, in its
schools, 'the Bible shall be read, and there
shall ho given such explanations and such in-
struction therefrom in the precepts of religion
and morality as are suited to the capacities of
children; and whereas all religious instruc-
tion is, under the Education Act of 1870, ex-
cluded from the cognizance of her Majesty's
Inspectors, it is incumbent upon the Board to
provide for some efficient inspection of such
religious instruction as is given in its schools,
and that it be referred to the School Manage-
ment Committee to consider a scheme for such
inspection, and to report thereon.''

A meeting was held at the Lambeth Baths

Resolutions declaring that women being

were sure to suffer from legislation, and

seconded, and adopted.
The Chairman accounted for the thin at-

"Singing Pilgrim," had drawn off a crowded
audience to the Surrey Chapel. He (the
Chairman) should not bind himself to every-
thing that might be said at the meeting, but
to the broad principle of the eligibility of
women for the franchise he gave his entire ad-
hesion. Ho cited the fact that women were
doctors, journalists, and periodical writers,
and it was therefore absurd to suppose that
they could not rationally use the Parlia-
mentary franchise.
il.The first resolution waq moved by Mr.'

One or two other speakers having addressed

usual vote of thanks to the Chairman terinina.

CONFERENCE AT BIRMINGHAM ON
DIRECT LABOUR REPRESENTATION.

DEAN, SIR,-

The demand everywhere of the artisans (Implored
our great centres of industry for direct representation of '
labour has developed into such an active life during the
existence of the present Parliament that it has best
deemed advisable by the Labour Representation League
at a preliminary meeting of Joint Committees, held in
Birmingham, October 16th, 1872, to summon a Conference

the same day, in the Great Hall, to which all sovietise
and friends favourable to the cause of Labour representa-
tion shall be invited.
The proposed object of the Conference is to devise a
plan of united action for the purpose of ensuring the
return to the next Parliament of some numb era belonging
to the ranks of Labour.
This question has assumed a much 'greater Importance
and consistency during the last four years than hereto-

articles.title: SATURDAY, DECEMBER 7, 1872.
articles.text:
SATURDAY, DECEMBER 7, 1872.

THE STRIKE OF THE GAS STOKERS.

Woincrwo men, it may be admitted, ought
to be well assured that they have- just
ground, and no other remedy, before they
betake themselves to a strike. It is a very
infectious example, as we see in its being
followed by every description of depend ants
upon manual labour or tbodily exertion.
There would, of course, be little sense in
throwing up work if those who took that
course had not persuaded themselves that
their services would not be very well dispensed
with. This has been the calculation of the
London Gas Stokers among the rest. But the
action which they have taken is of a sort
adapted to come home to the general public
more quickly and more keenly than in most
analogous oases. It is not, however, that they
wish to see the metropolis thrown into utter
darkness, and given up to thieves. Their
reckoning, doubtless, is, that, to avoid all such
inconvenience and exposure, the Companies ,
will be fain to concede their demands. Sup-
posing them to have an intelligent acquaint-
ance with the leading facts of their own ,
business, they may further be supposed to see
more clearly than some other craftsmen can,
the probable effect of their withdrawment from
their respective works. Even outsiders can
appreciate the meaning of house-to-house
visits by agents of the Companies, entreating
men of business to consume as little gas as
possible, and, in oases where long
.and late
hours are unavoidable, to shut off the gas
altogether and substitute candles. There
may, indeed, be no great conjuring about the
work of a stoker; bat, even in the simplest
and rudest forms of employment, there is
always a wide differenoe between the raw
recruit and the experienced expert.
The stokers on strike are, at any rate, very
reasonable. They assert the right of union;
and that it is too late to attempt to deny to
any class in the community whatever. Let
this principle be aoknowledged by reinstating
those men who have been turned adrift for
being in union; and as to all the rest, the
oomplainants are quite ready to abide by the
award of half-a-dozen arbitrators chosen by
the Companies and by their own committee.

The masters, however, cling to the hope that,
helped by the patience and the forbearance of
their customers, they shall tide over the diffi-
culty, filling with new men the vacant places,
and getting them soon familiar with their
work. As friends to all, and enemies to
none, we are glad to have the assurance of
those who pretend to speak for the general
public, that, although in private and public
circles an approach to something like " semi-
darkness " has been experienced, good humour
is preserved, and no fear excited. We under-
stand pretty well what is meant by old gen-
tlemen at their clubs " bluntly condemning"
the whole generation of stokers; but the com-
panies will fall into mistake if they rest their
cause upon such props. At present there is a
nearly universal preference of gas to any other
light ; and until invention or discovery finds a
better, it will be the wisdom of the companies
to encourage consumption and to maintain the
supply. The way to do this is to deal fairly
and reasonably by the hands employed in
every department of their works.

SO far as the Directors of the company, where
it commenced, are concerned, they seem to have
adopted the despicable example of the police
authorities by discharging an individual or
two who were prominent amongst the men
when urging their demands.
There is something inconceivably base in
such conduct. It is cowardly and malignant,
and never can have any other effect than that
of begetting and perpetuating the very worst
feelings between employers and employed, and
so long as a spark of honour remains amongst
working men it will, and ought to be, vigo-
rously resisted. At the same time we say that
the method of resistance should be the wisest
and best that can possibly be employed.

In the interest of the men themselves we
say they ought not to run their heads against
stone walls. What they have to do is not to
say to those in authority over thorn—" You
shall not discharge these men"—or, having dis-
charged them, " you must take them back."
Such a course only, at the best, gives tem-
porary protection, as the power of discharge
being necessarily and properly in the hands of
employers, sooner or later they will exercise it
to the injury of the offending party. Cases of
this sort, as we have already pointed out,
ought to be met by compensation. The em-
ployer discharges the man as a punishment,
and the men, in such a ease, should show that
it is no punishment whatever, but, if anything,
a gain. In this way, without any collision
between employer and employed, without the
loss of a day's work to the men, and what is
of great importance without any inconvenience
to the public, the objects of the employer may
be quietly defeated. A week's wages of the
gas stokers of London would give more money
to a fund of this kind ten times over than
could be called for, as one of its first effects
would be to put a stop for ever to this most
cowardly and reprehensible practice of dis-
charging men because they act in the interest
of their fellows. We ask those who take an
active part amongst working men for the pro-
motion of the interests of industry to consider
this. Striking, oven if victory was certain, is
a most wasteful and extravagant proceeding.

THE COMING STRUGGLE IN FRANCE.

WE regret to head our continued remarks
on what is passing in France with words so
ominous; and we even trust, that the friends
at °nee to peace, true order,. and real liberty
in that country, will yet be so helped by im-
palpable but all-powerful influences, ever
attendant upon pure and good causes and
those who further them, as to triumph over
the :difficulties that beset it and them, and
bring the ship through the surges and the
breakers into the safe and quiet harbour.
Again, however, the steps of the conflict
among parties are so ordered in point of time
as to leave us unable to give the complete and
decisive information we desire to put before
our anxious readers. The Committee on
whose Report so much depends, was to bo
nominated on Thursday in this week; and,
consequently, at the moment of writing, we
cannot state the result. Telegrams speak, in-
deed, of ' the "great debate" on Friday the
29th ult. ; but, though the occasion was great
and the speech of the PRESIDENT of the

REPUBLIC quite equal to the occasion and to
his best fame, there can hardly be said to have
been a debate. It is not in the French nature,
especially under excitement, to debate ques-
tions as we understand and practise the art.
The height to which angry passions quickly
rise in the breasts of our lively neighbours,
borders, no doubt, upon volcanic heat; yet,
even then, the tribune of the National Assem-
bly is as an open orator, by means of which
the solid structure of the nation may be saved
from convulsion and disruption. It is ominous
of no good when the leaders of the aristocratic
opposition evince a disposition to take critical
divisions without making speeches.
On that memorable Friday the speech of M.
TurEns was followed by a division in his
favour; but the part he takes must have
derived immensely more from the moral
weight of his own words than from a majority
of only three dozen in a house of seven
hundred members. The speech remains; but,
on the very next day, the majority of thirty-
six was °hanged into a minority of 6 against
the PRESIDENT'S Government in a house this
time of six hundred members. The hundred
who abstained from voting, whatever
their explanations may be, cannot mate-
rially affect in just interpretation the
reverse which changes an uncertain victory
into a positive defeat. But, in saying defeat,
we do not mean to credit the vote of censure
of which M. LEFIIINC, Home Minister, became
the scapegoat, as much of a victory to the
Right who, not without help from the Left
Centre, achieved it. If
.thirty-six could not
end the contest for the PRESII)ENT, much less
could an odd six be expected to drive him
even to resign, not to say succumb. It seems,
on the contrary, that the later vote has but
given an impulse to those manifestations of
Republican feeling on the part of the towns,
which it was the real object of the lturals to
cheek. If the Friday vote evinced a shrink-
ing on their part from the last extreme, the
Saturday vote showed that they had recovered
their reckless audacity. The complexion of
the Committee chosen this Thursday will
reveal what impression, if any, has been made
upon them by the firm attitude of the urban
part of the nation and the chief whom this
very majority were fain to place and to keep
over it. The legion of bad passions must have
gained complete possession of minds which,
under existing circumstances within and
without, shall not flinch from dismissing the
men who, whatever his prejudices, has, in
extreme old age, kept things together for the
two most trying years in the experience of
France.

To throw the Pact of Bordeaux in M.
TIIIRII.9'B teeth is one proof how lost to political
shame and deceney the French Dukes and
Squires are become. They, at any rate, have
not been conspicuous for their observance of
that agreement. As for him, ho is, by their
own vole, President of the Republic deActo ;
and to tell an iron-and-clay body of hetero-
geneous men that a Republic de leo is the
only thing possible so long as they, among
themselves, have three Kingßrigs claiming
one crown, is not to take the [constitution of
the Republic by the nation's voice out of the
forming hands of its chosen representatives.
At any rate M. Turns must not be taunted
with having gone out of his province by a set
of men who, in a formal report, which should
have been solemn, deliberately talk, not of
convincing, net of persuading, not of concilia-
ting, not even of expostulating with the party
of the Republic,: but only of extinguishing
them by force of arms
Although, however, the vote to which M.
LEFRANC offered himself in sacrifice disclosed
that dementation of the majority which in old
Rome was held to herald destruction by the
gods, the issue will proceed upon the com-
position of the committee named to consider
M. Duntrities successful amendment, and the
tenour of their report upon it. Surely those
deputies who have clear and cool heads will
have been careful, so far as they are considered,
to avoid the nomination of men whose brains
are fevered and confused. From a delirious
,committee nothing can be expected but fire-
brands, arrows, and death. Wise men, on the
contrary (and are there not two
.dozen such
in all Versailles will consider wisely of their

.9

doings. They will bear in mind, to begin
with, that the Government, through their
MINISTER of JUSTICE, accepted the leading idea
of M.,BsinrE's report, the principle, that is, of
Ministerial Responsibility. What they pro-
posed, and what the Assembly assented to,
was, that a committee of thirty should prepare
a Bill, dealing, indeed, with Ministerial re-
sponsibility, but also with the functions of all
public authorities. The effect would be, to
give to the Assembly, even as it is, the whole
range of constitutional questions adduced by
the PRESIDENT in his Message and urged by
him in his speech. This, which should have
satisfied the Rural:3, was carried in spite of
thorn; and they will evince a return to sense
for which nobody, not even themselves, gives
them credit, should they be found to have
accepted theinevitable, and to have contributed
to the formation of a committee whose report
may be in some way harmonised with M,
DITFAURE'S amendment. The natural eager-
ness of the Left for a Dissolution will, at the
same time, make it hard for them to bear any
such middle course as will leave constitutional
questions to the vote of the Assembly as it is.
But the Assembly will not dissolve itself; and
how can M. Turns, as its own nominee dis-
solve it; or what wouldbe the effect if,
disregarding that fact, he should attempt a
Dissolution by the assumption of Dictatorship.
Ile evidently shrinks from any such course,
as is testified by the feelers which continue
to be put out for a gradual renovation of the
Assembly. In the present temper of parties,
or, rather, of factions, even a General Election
appears full of dread, while a certain number
of elections from year to year would afford such
indications of the state of opinion in the
country as might teach the Rurals if they have
any docility. But, in fact, them are two
nations in France; and, with one of the two,
there are priests.

articles.text:
HORNCE GREELEY.

THE death of Houkci.: GREELEY will suggest
many reflections, not only in regard. to the life
and struggles of the man, but also in relation
to the institutions of a country whore such a
life and such struggles were possible to one
of his birth and culture. A farm lad, a
printer's boy, a journalist, in all the stages of
that most precarious profession, and ultimately
a candidate for the prosidenoy of the United
States, where, perhaps, the over-fatigue rather
than the failure, caused his death.
Had this man been born in England it is
almost certain he would have commenced
active life by scaring birds from the fields of
his father's master, and without exercising any
influence on the lives of his fellow creatures,
would have fiuished his days in the workhouse,
without anybody being aware of his departure
beyond the parish doctor, the nurse, and
the guardians. This may be fairly predicted.
It is not to consider too curiously to consider
so." In America, HORACIE GREELEY made
advances merely such as multitudes of his class
make. In getting on in the world he did
what millions of poor men's children do every
generation in the United States of America.
In Hampshire, Wiltshire, or Dorsetshire, he
would have done as the multitudes of farm
labourers do, and there the matter would have
ended. If his fate had been cast in Bucking-
hamshire, Mr. DISRAELI: possibly might, ten
years sine°, have presented him with a pair of
corduroy trowsers and 10s., for bringing up his
family without troubling the parish.
Luckily for him it was not so. Ile was
born in a country that cares for the education
of its poorest, and where, having received the
rudiments of education, he became a devourer
of books, and through them a sharer in the
world's knowledge and thought, and a capable
combatant in the struggles going on around
him for extending and securing the growing
liberties of the world. It may be said of
HonAou GREELEY, that lie was a consistent
advocate of negro emancipation, and though a
protectionist, was so on grounds more ex.
°usable in America than they could possibly
be in England. In the ordinary moaning of
the term he was not a party man; through
life hie conduct was allied to principle, and in
all the struggles he passed through, Which-
ever side he took, his aim was to exalt what
he believed to he the truth in a spirit as free

from personal passion or personal interest as
possible.
Td. opposing GRANT for the presidency he
made a very grave mistake, which, after so
long a life of earnest, honest, and usefol
labour, was to be deplored. OnAr's adminis
tration of the affairs of the country naay not
613'01 that is desirable, but his defeat, if such
tithing were possible, would have been an act
of national ingratitude, and worse than this,
it would have given encouragement and hope
to a spirit yet active in the Southern States,
which, politically, socially, and morally, is
perhaps the most detestable by which the
human mind has ever been influenced. The
renunciation of all future thought of office on
the part of HonAcE GREELEY' after his defeat
was pathetic, and his death following so
quickly upon this gives it a tragic touch of
painful melancholy. The at-one-time farm-
lad, openly, by sanction of law, reaching out
for the temporary sovereignty of his country,
and when missing his aim, lying down to die,
has something in it as an historical, lesson,
finer and more ennobling than the conquest
and subsequent plunder of the Norman Wm-
mar ; and whatever their drawbacks may
be, fills us with admiration for institutions,
which, in the conquests of the mind, or in the
acquisition of wealth and power, throws the
arena equally open to all. The solid worth to
be attained by sueh a sound human competi-
tion must in the end carry the day against the
filiegree,the frippery, and the feathers--backed
by sordid enough notions of solid cash—for
which the contests in our old European monar-
chies are carried on.

ECONOMY.
TIIE Marquis of SALISBURY is troubled
because the Liberals spend largely on the
army and navy without doing much good to
the nation by suoh expanditure. This is
perfeotly true; but we want to know what
the noble MA.Boante would do to curtail this
expenditure. If our contending political
parties will consent to make the expenditure
on the army and navy the question upon
which to light their battle for public: favour,
the nation will be delighted to give its support
to .that which can do most for the least
money.

In a contention of this kind, however, we can-
not be satisfied with empty words. The Marquis
of fluismiar must take dates and figures,
and point out where present extravagance is
to be found, how it has arisen, and in what
way it, can be corrected. In 1788—not one
hundred years ago—the taxes from all ,sourcea

is most melanchOlyl to eonsider, something like

ought, to be the conditions and cost of good
givernmetithas never been the question with

The interesting problem with them has always
been, how taxation could be made to keep
pana`with the power of the nation to pay it;
how, year by year, the increasing 'population
and the growing wealth of the country could
be made to contribute, not to the growing' re-
quirements of the nation, but to the insatiable .
wants of the governing classes, Who; by
handing the family property over to the eldest
salmi-left the younger branches of our great
!entities dependant on public plunder.
Our army and navy estimates now amount

quis of SALT ax inform us how they are to be

an astonishing fact in Our- history; but

far the proteotion of the lingltsh people from

articles.title: PUESIDENT'S MESSA.GE,
articles.text:
THE PUESIDENT'S MESSA.GE,

THE message of General GIILNT, as Presi-
dent of the great American Republic, is worth
quietly thinking over. Above all, as an ex-
position of the actual condition of a great free
nation, it deserves to be contrasted with tho
speeches and addresses of European Sovereigns
when "saying their say" as to the condition of
their several countries. What these dun-
nients reveal is worth volumes of discussion
as to the relative value of Monarchical and
Republican institutions.
In America there is nothing to be considered
but the best means of securing the moral and
material progress of the nation. That country
has neither revolutions in prospect, nor wars
threatening; its questions of disputed boun-
dary are all settled; its classes are united; its
rival trading interests are gradually adjusting
themselves. In fact, the pursuit of industry in
peace, and the progress of civilization by the
cultivation of literature and science, seem to
be the only work in which the American
nation is engaged ; and it may be said that
these various occupations are carried on
under the protection of laws made for the
advantage of all.
Where in Europe shall we find anything
corresponding to this ? In 11u95ia, an enormous
and crushing despotism, in which the will of
the Estrzliois is everything, the equity and
power of the law nothing. In Prussia, two
sinister forces fighting• for the mastery, with
no absolute security for justice or liberty for
the people whichever wins. In France—
what P--Nobles without nobility; the Lords
of Estates violent for the interests of their
class, careless as to the peace and welfare of
their country; Monarchists and Imperialists
conspiring to sot up their old foul, grinning
mud gods for the profit belonging to the
superstitions connected with them. In
England, an appalling contrast of riebea and
poverty; class strifes, with small prospect of
their disoontinuanca ; the crushing expense
of defensive and offensive armaments, with
no reasonable hope of that spirit of confidence
between the nations of luope which may
enable them 0, ellteitain thoughts of mutual
disarmament. . •
In the calculation on both sides, there is a
decided balance in favour of• America; and
this balance is not the result of any reasoning
on political systems, but on the past develop-
ment of fads in connection, with both systems,
as shown in thapregress of society•;--rt develop.
moat which, as it go4se on, must settle the dist,
put() asbetween Republicanism and hionarOhy,,
quite independent of the bias of prejudiee, or
the deduetions of logic.

HE? WORTH 'DIXON f AND THE "PALL

MALL GAZETTE."

WHAT is a libel ? Some time ago the
keeper of a railway refreshment-counter suc-
ceeded in getting damages from a person who
found fault with his sandwiches in one of our
newspapers. Tradesmen who• ordinarily oo-
cupy the jury-box are sensitive when shop-
keepers' wares are ittaeked. To say that
sausages or sandwiehes are unfit to eat, may
not be done with impunity; but to say that a
writer's works are unfit to read is 'quite a
different thing, and may be done without hesi-
tation or fear of any kind. The jury that
tried the ease of Dixox v. WITTE, by giving Mr.
Duos' a farthing damages, and the privilege
of paying his own costs, have justified this
theory, and for the future it may be taken for
granted that any writer or any publio man
who has the temerity to deal in ideas. must
,make up bis mind sot only to have his books

or his spoken words denounced as immoral or
dangerous, should any person think pro-
per to do so, but must submit in addition to
any misrepresentation or abuse that may be
flung ,at 'him by any unserupulous rival or
enemy who may owe him a grudge.
We are disposed to go almost any length in
defence of the liberty of the press; but we do
not include in this the liberty of defamation.
Nor do we object to anonymous writing in our
newspapers, but we submit that personal at-
tacks shonld never be made behind such a
shield. fl'o doubt in this case the Pall lfail
Oazette committed an offence not only against
Mr, llE.ewosni DIXON, but against fairness
and honour, worse than anything done by Mr.
Duce& against morality. In proof of this it is

We mily say, nevertheless, that whatever Mr.

this wretched libel did not believe it himself—

nized by the public anywhere in that character;

It ought to be unnecessary to inform even
those who take theleast interest in PIO h matteri

is utterly false—has not a shadow of foundation
in truth, The history and character of the

persons who have travelled in America have

everybody knew that absolute celibacy was
,the foundation and keystone or their system.
, There can be no excuse for this sort of igno-
rance or malioiousnees;Whichever it may be.
To make an untrue charge, and to give it
colour by other untruths ought not to receive
any sort of countenance ai a practice in the
newspaper press of the country from any jury
of Englishmen, whatever their irritation
against supposed moral offendera. We know
nothing whatever personally of Mr. Dricx,
nor Amid we say a word in his defence were
he what the writer in the 'Pall Mull Gasells
declares him to be. In this case, however, it
is plain that the peceant paper has escaped a
punishment its turpitude very richly merited,
and we feel it our duty to say so.

A. breath, like the wind's breath, may carry
A name far and wide,
But the measure of time does not tally
With any man's pride.
'Tis not a wild chorus of praises,
Nor chance, nor yet fate—
'Tis the manhood born with him, and in him,
That makes the man great.
And when in the calm self-possession

True manhood confers,
The man is stretched out to that measure
Fame claims him for hors.
Too proud to fall back on achievement,
With work in his sight,
His triumph may not overtake him

articles.text:
A FEARFUL BALLOON ADVEN-

TUBE.

We are not related. His name is John Griffiths,
and I am William Waldur ; and we called our-
selves the Patagonian Brothers, because it looked
well in the bills and pleased the public. We met
by chance, about six years since, on the race-course
at Doncaster, and so took a sort of mutual liking,
and went partners in a tour through the midland
counties. We had never seen or heard of each
other up to that time; and, though we became
good friends' were never greatly intimate. I knew
nothing of his past life, nor ho of mine, and I never
asked him a question on the subject. I am parti-
cular to have this all clear from the beginning ;
for I am a plain man telling a plain story, and I
want no one to misunderstand a word of what I
am about to relate.

We made a little money by our tour. It was
not much; but it was more than either of us had
been able to earn before; so we agreed to stay
together and try our fortune in London. This
time we got an engagement at Astley's for the
winter, and, when the summer came, joined a
travelling circus, and roamed about as before.
The circus was a capital thing—a republic, so to
say, in which all were equals. We had a mane•
ger, to whom we paid a fixed salary, and the rest
went shares in the profits. There were times
when we did not even clear our expenses; there
were towns where we made ten and fifteen pounds
a night; but the bad luck wont along with the
good, and on the whole we prospered.
We stayed with the company two 'years and a
half in all, and played at every town between York
and London. During that time we had found lei-
sure to improve. We knew each other's weight
and strength now to a hair, and grew bolder with
experience; no that there was scarcely a new feat
brought out anywhere which we did not learn,
oven to the " perch() " business, and the trick of
walking, head downwards, on a marble ceiling.
The fact is that we were admirably matched,
which, in our profession, is the most important
point of all. Our height was the same, to the
sixteenth of an inch, and we wore not unlike in
figure. If Griffiths possessed a little more mug-
cular strength, I was the more active, and even
that difference was in our favour. I believe that,
in other respects, we suited each other equally
well, and I know that, for the three years and a
half which we had spent together (counting from
our first meeting at Doncaster down to the time
when we dissolved partnership with the circus
folks), we had never had an angry word. Grif-
fiths was a steady saving, silent follow enough,
with little grey eyes, and heav7 black brows. I
remember thinking, once or twice, that he was not
quite the sort of person I would like for an enemy;
but that was in reference to no act of his, and only
a fancy of my own. For myself,! can live with
any one who is disposed to live with me, and love
peace and good-will bettor than anything in the
world.

• _
We had now grown so expert that we resolved
to better ourselves and return to London, which
we did somewhere about the end of February, or
the beginning of March. We put up at a little
inn in the Borough; and, before a week was over,
found ourselves engaged at the Belvidere Tavern,
at a salary of £7 a week. Now this was a groat
advance upon all our previous gains; and the tavern
was by no means a bad place for the founding of a
theatrical reputation.
Situated half-way between the West-end and
the city, surrounded by a densely populated neigh-
bourhood, and lying in the very path of tha
Omnibuses, this establishment was one of the most
prosperous of its class. There was a theatre, and
a concert-room, and a garden, where dancing, and
smoking, and rifle-shooting, and supper-eating was
going on from eight to twelve o'clock every night
all through the summer, which made the place a
special favourite with the working classes.
Here, then, we were engaged (Griffiths and I),
lota a promise that our salary should be raised if
we proved attractive; and raised it soon was, for

we drew enormously. We brought out the perche
and the ceiling business; came down in the midst
of fireworks, from a platform higher than the roof
of thB theatre; and, in short, did everything that
ever yet was done in our line—aye, and did it well,
too; though perhaps it is not my place to say so.
At all events the great coloured posters were
pasted up all over the town, and our salary was
increased to £l5 a week, and the gentleman who
writes about the plays in the Sunday Snub was
pleased to observe that there was no performance
in London half so wonderful as that of the Pata-
gonian Brothers—for which I take this oppor-
tunity to thank him kindly.
We lodged (of course, together) in a quiet street
on a hill, near Islington. The house was kept by
Mrs. Morrison, a respectable, industrious woman,
whose husband had been a gas-fitter at one of the
theatres, and who was now left a widow with one
only daughter just nineteen years of age. She was
very good, and very pretty. She was christened
Alice, but her mother called her Ally, and we soon
fell into the same habit; for they were very
simple, friendly people, and we were soon as good
friends as if we had all been living together in the
same house for years.
I am not a good hand at telling a story, as, I
dare say, you have found out by this time—and,
indeed, I never did sit down to write one out before
—so I may as well come to the point at once, and
confess that I loved her. I also fancied, before
many months were over, that she did not altogether
dislike me ; for a man's wits are twice as sharp
when he is in love, and there is not a blush, or a
glance, or a word, that he does not contrive to
build some hope upon. So one day, when Griffiths
was out, I went down stairs to the parlour, where
she was sitting by the window sowing, and took a
chair beside her.

"Ally, my dear," said I, stopping her right hand
from working, and taking it up in both of mine,
"Ally, ray dear, I want to speak to you."
She blushed, and turned pale, and blushed again,
and I felt tho pulses in her little soft hand throb-
bing like the heart of a frightened bird, but she
never answered a syllable.
"Ally, my dear, said I, "I am a plain man.
lam thirty-two years of age. I don't know how
to flatter like some folks, and I have had very little
book-learning to speak of. But, my dear, I love
you; and, though I don't pretend that you are
the first girl I over fancied, I can truly say that
you are the first I over cared to make my wife. So,
if you'll take me, such as I um, I'll be a true hus-
band to You as long as I live."
What answer she made, or whether she spoke at
all, is more than I can undertake to tell; for my
ideas were all confused, and I only remember that
I kissed her, and felt very happy, and that when
Mrs. Morrison came into the room, she found mo
with my arm clasped round my darling's waist.
I scarcely know when it was that I first noticed
the change in John Griffiths; but that it was some-
where about this time I am tolerably certain. It
is hard to put looks into words, and to make ac-
count of trifles that, after all, are matters of feel-
ing more than matters of fact; but others saw the
change AS well as myself, and no one could help
observing that he grow to be more silent and un-
sociable than ever. He kept away from home as
much as possible. He spent all his Sundays out,
starting away the first thing after breakfast, and
not coming back again till close upon midnight.
He even put an end to our old friendly custom of
walking home together after our night's work was
over, and joined a sort of tap-room club that was
kept up by a dozen or so of idle fellows belonging
to the theatre. Worse than this, ho scarcely ex-
changed a word with me from morning till night,
even when we were at meals. He watched me
about the room as if I had been a thief. And some-
times, though I am sure I never wronged him
willingly in my life, I caught him looking at me
from under those black brows of his as if he hated
me.

More than once I laid my hand upon his sleeve
as ho was hurrying away on Sundays, or turning
off towards the club-room at night, and said,
" Griffiths, have you got anything against me ?" or,
" Griffiths, won't you come home to a friendly
glass with me to-night ?" But he either shook me
off without a word, or muttered some sulky denial
that sounded more like a curse than a civil answer;
so I Fot tired of peace-making at last, and lot him
go his own way, and choose his own company.
The summer was already far advanced, and our
engagemeat at the Belvidere had well-nigh ended,
when I began to buy the furniture, and Ally to
prepare her wedding things. Matters continued
the same with John Griffiths: but, when the day
was fixed, I made up my mind to try him once
again, and invite him to the church and the dinner.
The carcumstances of that invitation are as clear
in my memory as if the whole affair had taken
place this morning.
It was on the 29th of July (I am particular
about dates), and there had been a general
call to rehearsal at one o'clock that day. The
weather was warm and hazy, and I started early
that I might not go in late or tired; for I knew
that, what with the rehearsal and the new piece,
and the Terrific Descent, I should have enough to
do before my day's work was over. The conse-
quence was that I arrived about twenty minutes
too soon. The gardens had a dreary look by day-
light; but they were pleasanter, anyhow, than the
theatre; so I loitered up and down among the
smoky trees, and watched the waiters polishing the
stains off the tables in the surnmer-houses, and
thought how shabby the fountains looked when
they were not playing, and what misetiblo gim-
crack concerns were the Stalactite Caves and the
Cosmorarnic Grottoes, and all the other attractions
which looked so tine by the light of coloured lamps
and fire-works.

Well, just as I was sauntering on, turning these
things over in my mind, whom should I mee in one
of the summer-houses but John Griffiths ! 0 IV
lying forward upon the table with his face resting
upon his clasped bands, sound asleep. Au empty
ale-bottle and glass stood close beside him, and his
stick had fallen near his chair. I could not be
inistsken in him, though his face was hidden;

so I went up and touched him smartly on the
shoulder.
"A fine morning, John !" says I. "I thought I
was here early; but it seems that you were before
me, after all.'
lie sprang to his feet at the sound of my voice
as if he had been struck, and then turned imps-
tiontly away.
"What did you wake me for?" he said sill-
lonly.
‘. Because I have news to tell you. You know
that the 6th of August will be our last night here.
'Well, mate, on the 7th, please God, I'm going to
be married, and—"
"Curse you," he interrupted, turning a livid
face upon me, and an eye that glared like a tiger's.
"Curse you! How dare you come to me with that
tale, you smooth-faced hound ?—to me, of all men
living ?"
I was so little prepared for this burst of pas-
sion that I had nothing to say; and so he went
on:—

"Why can't you let me alone? What do you
tempt me fur? I've kept my hands off you till
now. . .

He paused and bit his lip, and I saw that he
was trembling from head to foot. lam no coward
—it's not likely that I should be a Patagonian
Brother if I was; but the sight of his hatred
seemed to turn me, for the moment, quite sick and
giddy.
"My God!" said I, leaning up against the table,
"what do you mean? Are you mad ?"
He made no answer; but looked straight at me,
and then walked away. I don't know how it was;
but from that moment I knew all. It was written,
somehow, in his face.
"Oh, illy dear I" I said to myself with a kind
of groan, and sat down on the nearest bench; I be-
lieve that, at that moment, I scarcely knew where
I was, or what I was doing.
I did not see him again till we met on the stage,
about an hourafterwarde, to go through our scene in
the rehearsal. It was a grand Easter piece with
a great deal of firing, and real water, and a live
camel in the last act; and Griffiths and I were
Mozambique slaves, performing before the Rajah
in the Hall of Candelabras. Excepting that it
cost a great deal of money, that is all I ever knew
about the plot; and, upon my word, I don't be-
lieve that anybody else knew much more. By this
time I had, of course, recovered my usual com-
posure; but I could see that Griffiths had been
drinking, for Ms face was flushed and his balance
unsteady. When the rehearsal was over, the ma-
nager called us into his private room and brought
out a decanter of sherry, with which, I must say,
he was always as liberal as any gentleman could
be.

" Patagonians," says he, "for he had a wonder-
fully merry way with him, and always called us
by that name,,' I suppose you would make no
objection to a little matter of extra work and extra
pay on the 6th—just to end the season with some-
thing stunning—hey
"No, no, Sir, not we," replied Griffiths, in a
sort of hearty manner that wasn't natural to him.
"We're ready for anything. Is it the gying busi-
ness you spoke about the other day '
"Better than that," said the manager' filling up
the glasses. "It's a new French feat that has
never yet been done in this emintry, and they call
it the trapeze:
.Patagonians, your health!"
. . .

So we ilrank his in-return, and then he explained
all about it. It was to be an exhibition of pos-
turing and a balloon ascent both in ono. At some
distance below the car was to be secured a tri-
angular wooden frame-work, which frame-work
was called a trapeze. From the lower pole, or
base of this triangle, one of us was to be suspended,
with a ligature of strong leather attached to his
ankle, in case of accidents. Just as the balloon
was rising and this man ascending head down-
wards, the other was to catch him by the hands
and go up also, having, if he preferred it, some
band or other to bind him to his companion. In
this position we were then to go through our
customary performances, continuing theta so long
as
,the balloon remained in sight.

"Alt this," continued the- manager, "sound!
much more dangerous than it really is. The
motion of a balloon through the air is so steady
and imperceptible that, but for the knowledge of
being up above the housetop; you will perform al-
most as comfortably as in the gardens. Besides, I
am speaking to brave men who know their business,
and are not to be dashed by a trifle—hey, Pats-
gonians ?" _

- Griffiths brought his hand down heavily upon
the table, and made the glasses ring again.
" I'm ready, Sir," said he, with an oath. "I'm
ready to do it alone, if any man here is afraid to go
with me !"

Ho looked at me as he said this with a sort of
mocking laugh that brought the blo3d up into my
face.

"If you moan that for me, John," said I, quick-
ly, " I'm no more afraid than yourself; and, if
that's all about it, I'll go up to-night ! "
If I was to try from now till this thy next year,
I never could describe the expression that came
over his face as I spoke those words. It seemed
to turn all the currents of my blood, I could not
understand it then; but I understood it well enough
afterwards. - -

Well, our manager was mightily pleased to find
us so willing, and a very few more words ended
the matter. Mr. Staines and his famous Wurtem-
burg balloon were to ba engaged; fifteen hundred
additional coloured lamps were to be hired;
and Griffiths and I were to receive twelve pounds
apiece for the evening, over and above our general
salary.
Poor Ally! In the midst of the excitement I
had forgotten her, And it was not till I was out
of the theatre and walking slowly homeward
that I remembered she must be told. Per my
own part, I did net believe there will the slightest
danger; but I knew how her fears would magnify
everything, and the nearer I cause tewardb
islington the more uncomfortable I felt. After
all, 1 was such a coward—for I always am a
coward where women are coaecr4o4-4hat

could not tell her that day, nor even the next ;
and it was only on Sunday, when we were sitting
together after dinner, that I found courage to speak
of it. I bad expected something of a scene; but
I had no idea that she would have taken on as
she did, and I declare that, even then, if the posters
had not been already out and myself bound in
honour to act up to my engagement, I would have
declined the business altogether. Poor little, soft-
hearted darling! it was a sore trial to her and to
me also, and I was an inconsiderate idiot not to '
have thought of her feelings in the first instance.
But there was no help for it now; so I gave her
the only consolation in my power by solemnly
promising that I would be the first man tied to the
trapeze. It was, of course, the safest position, and
when I had assured her of this, she grew calmer.
On all other points I kept my own counsel, as you
may be certain; and as to John Griffiths, I 84W
less of him than ever. He even took his meals in
the city now, and during the seven days that
elapsed between the 29th and the 6th, never once
came face to face with me, except upon the stage.
I bad a hard matter to get away from home
when the afternoon of the 6th came round. My
darling clung about me as if her heart would break,
and although I did my beat to cheer her, I don't
mind confessing now that I went out and cried a
tear or two in the passage.
"Reap up your spirits, Ally, dear," ger I'
smiling, and kissing her the last thing before It:14
the house.
"And don't be spoiling
eyes in that way. Remember that want YOU to
look well, and that wo are to be married to-mor-
row !" your pretty

The multitude in the Belvidere Gardens was
something wonderful. Them they were--illeht
women, and children thronging the balconies, the
orchestra stairs, and every available inch of
ground; and there, in the midst of them, rolled
and swayed the huge Wurtemburg balloon, like a
sleepy, lolling giant. The ascent was fixed for six
o'clock, that we might come down again by day-
light; so I made haste to dress, and then went to
the green-room to hoar something of what was
going forward.
The manager was there, and three gentlemen
with him, namely, Colonel Steward, Captaia
Crawford, and Sydney Baird, Esquire. They were
fine handsome looking men, all three. I was going
to draw back when I saw them sitting there with
their wine and cigars; but they would have nis
in to take a glass of port, and shook hands with
me all round.

"Hero's health and success to you, my brave
fellow," says Colonel Steward, "and a pleasant
trip to us all !" and then I found that they were
going up in the oar with Mr. Staines.
And now, what with their light cheerful wsYs
and pleasant talking, and what with the glass of
wine that I had taken, and the excitement, and
the hum of voices from the crowd outside, I was
in first-rats spirits, and as impatient to be off as a
racer at the starting point. Presently one of the
gentlemen looked at his watch.

"What are we waiting for?" said ho. "It is
ten minutes peat six already."
And so it was. Ten minutes past the hour, and
Griffiths had not yet been seen or hoard of. Well,
we all grew very uneasy, and the crowd very
noisy, and so twenty minutes more went by.
Then we made up our minds to go without him,
and the manager made a little speech and ex-
plained it to the people; and then there was a
eheer, and a great bustle; and the gentlemen took
their seats in the car; and a hamper full of Cham-
pagne and cold chicken was put in with them
and I was made fast by one leg to the base of the
trapeze; and 111 r. Staines was just about to get in
himself and give the aignal to ant loose, when
who should we see forcing his way through the
crowd but Griffiths. .
Of course there was another cheer at this, and
a delay of eight or ten minutes more while he was
dressing. At last he came, and it was now just a
quarter to seven o'clock. Ile looked very sullen
when he found that he was to be the undermost;
but there was no time to change anything now,
even if I had been willing; so his left wrist and
my right were bound together by a leathern strap,
the signal was given, the band struck up, the
crowd applauded like macl, and the balloon rose
straight and steady above the heads of the people.
Down saek the trees and the fountains, and the
pavement of upturned faces. Down sank the roof
of the theatre, and fainter grew the sound of the
hurrahiug and the music. 'lle sensation was so
strange that, for the first moment, I was forced to
close my eyes, and felt as if I must fall and be
dashed to pieces. But that soon passed away, and
by the time we had risen to about three hundred
feet I WAS as comfortable A s if I had been born
and bred in the air with my head down-
wards.
Presently. we began our performances. Griffiths
was as cool as possible—l never saw him cooler—
and we went through every conceivable attitude;
now swinging by our hands, now by our feet, now
throwing somersaults one over the other. And
during the whole of this time the streets and
squares seemed to sink away to the right, and the
noises from the living world died on the air—and,
as I turned and slung, changing my position with
every minute, I caught strange fitting glimpses
of the sunset and the city, the sky and too river,
the gentlemen leaning over the car and the tiny
Passengers swarming down below like ants on an
ant-hill.

Thou the gentlemen grew tired of leaning over,
and began to talk and laugh, and busy themselves
over their !limper. Then the Surrey hilts drew
nearer, and the city s ink away to the right,
farther and farther. Then there wore nothing but
green fields with lines of railway crossing them
here and there ; and presently it grow quite damp
and misty, and we ceased to see anything, except
through breaks atal openings in the clouds.
" C 'me, John," says 1, 'Sour share uf this busi-
-11033 is done. Don't you think ws might as well
be getting into the car ?"
lie was hanging below just then, holding on by
ley two hands, and had been han.ing so (vice quiet
for some minutes. Ile didu't steal to uesrjflO

and no wonder, for the clouds were gathering
about us so thickly that even the voices of the
gentlemen up above grew mulled, and I could
hardly see for a yard before me in any direction.
So I called to him again, and repeated the ques-
*en.
He made no answer, but shifted his grasp from
my hand to my wrist, and then up to the middle
of my arm, so raising himself by degrees, till our
faces came nearly on a level. There he paused,
and I felt his hot breath on my cheek.
"William Waldur," said he, hoarsely, " wasn't
to-morrow to have been your wedding-day ?"
Something in the tone of his voice, in the
question, in the dusk and dreadful solitude, struck
me with horror. I tried to shake off his hands,
but he held too fast for that.
"Well, what if it was ?'' said I, after a moment.
"You needn't grip so hard. Catch hold of the
pole, will you? and let go of my arms."
He gave a short hard laugh, but never stirred.
" I suppose we're about two thousand feet high,"
says he, and it seemed to me that he had something
between his teeth. "If either of us was to fall,
he'd be a dead man before he touched the ground."
I would have given the world at that moment to
be able to see his face; but what with my own
head being downwards, and all his weight hanging
to my arms, I had no more power than an infant.
"John !" I exclaimed, "what do you mean ?
Catch hold of the pole, and let me do the same.
Alv head's on fire !"
"Do you see this F" said he, catching my arms
a couple of inches higher up, and looking right into
nav face. "Do you see this F"
It was a large, open clasp-knife, and he was
holding it with his teeth. His breath seemed to
hiss over the cold blood. "I bought it this
evening—l hid it in my belt— I waited till the
clouds came round and there was no soul to see.
Presently I shall cut you away from the balloon.
I took an oath that you should never have her, and
I mean to keep it !"
A dimness came over my eyes, and everything
grew red. I felt that in another minute I should
be insensible. He thought that I was so already,
and, letting my arms free, made a spring at the
pole overhead. ,
That spring saved Trio. Our wrists were bound
together, and as he rose he drew me along with
him; for I was so faint and giddy that I could
make no effort for myself.
I saw him hold by the pole with his left hand;
I saw him take the knife in his right; I felt the
cold steel pass between his wrist and mine, and
then
And then, the horror of the moment gave me
back my strength, and I clung to the frame-work
just as the thong gave way.
We were separated now, and I was still secured
to the trapeze by one ankle, He had only his
arms to trust to—and the knife.
Oh, the deadly, deadly strife that followed! it
sickens me to think of it. His only hope now
lay in the cursed weapon; and so, clinging to the
woodwork with ono hand, he strove to stab me
with the other.
It was livo or death now, and I grew desperate.
To feel his murderous clutch upon my throat, and,
in the silence of that hideous struggle, to hear
the report of a Champagne cork—followed by a
peal of careless laughter—overhead . . •
Oh, it was worse than death, a hundred times
over.
I cannot tell how long we clung thus, each with
a hand upon the other's throat. It may have been
only a few seconds; but it seemed like hours to
me. The question was simply which should be
strangled first.
Presently his grip relaxed, his lips became white,
and a shudder ran through every fibre of his body.
He had turned giddy.
Then a cry burst from him—a cry like nothing
human. He made a false clutch at the trapeze,
and reeled over. I caught him, just in time, by
the belt round his waist.
"It's all over with me," he Froaned between his
set teeth. "It's all—over—with me! Take your
revenge !" Then his head fell heavily back, and
he hung, a dead weight on may arm.
I did take my revenge ; but it was hard work,
and I was alreuly half exhausted. How I con-
trived to hold him up, to unbind my foot, and to
crawl, so laden, up the ropes, is more than I can
tell; but my presence of mind never failed me for
an instant, and I suppose the excitement gave me
a sort of false strength while it lasted. At all
events, I did it, though I now only remember
climbing over the basket-work, and seeing the
faces of the gentlemen all turned upon me as I
sank to the bottom of the car, scarcely more alive
than the burden in my arms.
Ho is a penitent man now, an Australian settler,
and is, I run told, doing well there
This is my story, and I have no more to tell.

DISTINCTIONS IN SNORING.
The variety of power in the nasal organ it
great. You have the piano snore, commencing on
a weak key and passing away into a thin whistle,
which we have mistaken for the wind playing
through the keyhole or some other cranny. Then
there is the great sonorous snore, pealing awfully
through the house in the silence of the night. We
once had a visitor with such gifted nostrils, and we
can depone, that although he did not awaken any
responsive concert in the pond, he set our two
terriers, at the dead of night, into a furious fit of
barking. It was a new terror to them, and we
had the greatest difficulty of explaining to Billy
and Pepper that no harm was meant—that no in-
vasion of the premises was threatened—that it was
vox et praterea nihil. 'rho great snore is often
varied by wild unearthly cadences harmonizing
with the howling wind without; and in listening
to such a performance, we are free to confess that
sometimes on our solitary pillow we have felt a
little eerie. But the most characteristic and beet
defined snore is the sudden, quick, convulsive snore,
properly described as a snort. It is as like as may
be to the snort of the war-horse, or to that of the
starting, struggling locomotive, for which it has
been more than once mistaken by a half-awake
traveller who had to go by arc early train. The lo-
comotive seems clearly to have copied from the
human engine. It is a vulgar error to suppose
that a largo proboscis is necessarily an organ of
groat power. On the contrary, in the hugh cavern
the air seems to lose itself; and we have seen an
insignificaat snub that would have outsnored the
most exaggerated Roman variety.
CHARACTER OF HAMLET.
'Hamlet loved Ophelia in his happy youth,
when all his thoughts were fair and sweet as she.
But his father's death,t,his mother's frailty, have
wrought sad alteration in his soul, and made the
very form of woman fearful and suspected. His
best affections are blighted, and Opholia's love,
that young and tender flower, escapes not the
general infection. Seemed not his mother kind,
faithful, innocent? And was she not married to
his uncle? But after the dread interview, the
fatal *unction, he is a man among whose thoughts
and purposes love cannot abide. He is a being
severed from human hopes and joys—vowed and
dedicated to other work than courtship and dalli-
ance. The spirit that ordained him an avenger,
forbade him to be a lover. Yet, with an incon-
staney as natural as it is unreasonable he clings
to what he has renounced, and sorely feels the re-
luctant repulse which Ophelia's obedience presents
to his lingering addresses. Lovers, even if they
have seen no ghosts, and have no uncles to slay,
when circumstances oblige them to discontinue
their suit, can ill endure to be anticipated in the
breach. It is a sorrow that cannot bear the
slightest show of unkindness. Hamlet, moreover,
though a tardy, is an impatient nature, that
would feel uneasy under the common process of
maidenly delay. Thus perplexed and stung, he
rushes into Opholia's chamber, and, in amazed
silence, makes her the confident of his grief and
distraction, the cause of which she must not know.
No wonder she concludes that he is mad for her
love, and enters readily into what to her appears
an innocent scheme to induce him to lighten his
overcharged bosom, and ask of her the peace
which, unasked, she may not offer. She steals
upon his solitude, while, weary of his unexecuted
task, he argues with himself the expediency of
suicide. Surprised as with a sudden light, his
first words are courteous and tender, till he begins
to suspect that she, too, is sent on to pluck out
the heart of his mystery; and then, actually mad-
dened by his self-imposed necessity of personating
madness, he discharges upon her the bitterness of '
blasted love, the agony of a lover's anger, as if de-
termined to extinguish in himself the last feeling
that harmonized not with his fell purpose of
revengeful justice. To me, this is the most terrifi-
cally affecting scene in Shakespeare. Neither
Lear nor Othello are plunged so deep in the gulf of
misery.—Coleridge.

Almost any one can be courteous in a neigh-

of time, or is disagreeable there itis made the beat of,
not the worst; even efforts are made to excuse it,
and show it is not felt; it is attributed to accident,
not to design; and this is not only easy but natu-

believe that what is so natural in the house of
another is impossible at home,
but maintain, with

-
be upheld in domestic society. husband as

willing to be pleased at home as he is anxious to
be plea-ed in a neighbour's house, and a wife as
intent on making things comfortable every day to
her family as on set days to her guests, cannot fail
to make home happy.

The organist of Bangor was a very great epicure,
and always gave minute directions as to the cook-
ing. One Sunday, however, being rather late, he
went to church without giving his usual instruc-
tions; and soon afterwards his wife discovered the
awkward dilemma in which his forgetfulness had
plunged her. She had therefore no alternative but
to send her little boy after him to church, to inquire
how his dinner must be cooked. When the boy
had got there, he found they had just commenced
the Te Deum ; and, fearing to wait until it was
finished, he crept up to his father, and commenced
singing in his ear, in the treble voice:

"My mother's bought a leg and a loin of mutton,
And what must she do with it ? "
The organist promptly replied to the lad's question
in the bass:

"She must boil tbe leg and roast the loin,

BIRDS AND FISIIRS.

Among birds are to be found families whose
decorations are quite inimitable by any material
that we arc acquainted with, be it even gems and
metals; whose song by its mere tone moves the
listener almost to tears, although ho is ignorant of
the exact sentiment that inspires the melodist.
Some, as the raven, are absolutely cosmopolitan in
their dispersion throughout the climates of our
planet. The four departments of material nature
popularly styled elements, seem open and accessible
to them—earth, air, water, ani flre almost, or heat
as hot as fire. Nor are there wanting to promote
our sympathy the qualities of acute perception,
docility, mimicry, even fun and humour, courage,
gallantry, strong affections—above all parental
love. What community of feeling can we enter into
with a fish ?—a creature that increases its kind with
little or no experience of the delights of mutual
and parental affection; brings forth by thousands
and hundreds of thousands at a time; eats its own
progeny indiscriminately with those of its neigh-
bour, showing no favour to either, just as they
are arriving at the most interesting stages of their
youth : that indulges a voracious appetite without,
as far as physiologists can judge, enjoying the
pleasures of taste; that dozes, indeed, now and
then, but never seems to know what a comfortable
night's rest is, though it may be torpid for a whole
winter; that has a chance, especially if it be
cartilaginous!), constituted, of living for centuries,
and yet is liable to be snapped up by its own
great grandfather without a moment's warning ?
